title: Present at Every Step
subtitle: Six Days with Brother Lawrence for the Camino Inglés
author: CaminoPlus

spans.t: This is a short book for a short road. It is made to go with the Camino Inglés, the English Way, a road of about a week, and it has six days: one to read for each day of walking, or six days at home, before the road or after it. If your walk turns out longer or shorter, nothing breaks. Read a day twice, leave one for later, or take two on a rest day.
Every day has a morning reading of about five minutes and an evening reflection of about three.
In the morning
there are three parts.

items.t: The passage.
A few lines from
The Practice of the Presence of God

, a small book of conversations and letters by a seventeenth-century lay brother in Paris. The words are quoted exactly as an old English edition printed them, old spellings and capital letters included. Read the passage twice, once for the sense and once for the sound, aloud if you can. The old wording makes you slow down, which suits it.
The reflection.

This part is ours, not Brother Lawrence's. It starts from something on the road, a chore, a wandering mind, a flat afternoon, and lets the passage open it. It tries to say what the passage says, to admit where it is hard, and to ask no more of an ordinary day than a day can give.
For the walk.
A question to carry for the next hour and one small practice that needs nothing but attention. Leave the notebook in the pack. These are better done on your feet.

spans.t: In the evening
there are two more.

items.t: At the end of the day.

A look back over the day you have just lived, with the morning's passage in mind. It is honest about tiredness, and it asks two or three gentle questions. You do not have to write anything down. They are questions to take to bed.
A short prayer.
Original, and short. If you pray, it is yours to use. If you pray in another way, change the words. If you do not pray, take it as a wish, said into the dark.

spans.t: A Christian book, and who it is for

Brother Lawrence was a Christian, a lay brother in a Catholic religious community, and everything he says is said to God and about God. The practice that gives his book its title, keeping himself in God's presence, is a Christian practice. We say so plainly so that nobody is surprised.

People walk the Camino for many reasons: faith, sport, grief, curiosity, a rest from work. All of them are welcome here. You do not need to share Lawrence's faith to keep him company for a week. What anyone can recognise is the shape of what he describes: small turnings of the attention, made often, with no fuss when you forget. If you borrow that shape without his name for God, borrow it knowing that it is a borrowing, and that he means a person, not a technique for calm. Where he is hard to follow, we say so.
The shape of the six days
The days do not follow the order of the original. They follow a walk.

items.t: Day 1, setting out.
How little is asked of you.
Day 2, the ordinary task.
The errand or chore you would rather not do.
Day 3, distraction and return.
The mind that runs off, and the way back.
Day 4, dryness.
The day when nothing is felt and the road goes on.
Day 5, the small kindnesses.
A straw on the path, a gate, a word.
Day 6, going on.
What is worth carrying home.

spans.t: The days are a shape, not a timetable. The book cannot know which day of your walk will be the flat one. Read the day that fits the day you are having. If you are tired, the passage and the prayer are enough, and the rest will keep until morning.
On the road and at home

Read the morning part wherever you stop: a bench, a bunk, a café table while the soup comes. Then put the phone away and take the question with you for an hour. Keep the evening part for last, once the boots are off. At home the pattern is the same, with tea in the morning and the evening before bed.
Two words you will meet. An
albergue
is the simple hostel where pilgrims sleep, often in bunks, often with a shared kitchen.
Buen Camino
is what walkers say to one another on the road, roughly, may your Way go well. Other words are explained where they first appear.
Read slowly. These are letters and notes, short on purpose, and they keep better one at a time.

chapters.title: About the book and its author

spans.t: The man
The Practice of the Presence of God

is the work of Brother Lawrence, though not in the way most books are the work of their authors. The title page of the edition we use calls him Nicholas Herman, of Lorraine. The preface says he had been a footman and a soldier, and that he was admitted as a lay brother among the barefooted Carmelites at Paris in 1666, and was afterwards known as Brother Lawrence.

Two of those terms need a gloss, and the gloss is ours, not the edition's. A lay brother is a member of a religious community who is not a priest and who does its practical work. The barefooted Carmelites are the Discalced Carmelites, a reformed branch of the Carmelite order, whose reform began in Spain in the sixteenth century.

The edition tells us a little more, and that is all we claim. The First Conversation reports him saying that at about eighteen, in winter, the sight of a tree stripped of its leaves, and the thought that leaves and fruit would return, gave him a lasting sense of God's power and care. He had been footman to a treasurer, and by his own account, as reported, "a great awkward fellow who broke everything". Later he worked in his community's kitchen and was sent out to buy its wine. The preface says he died at the age of eighty, and in the Seventh Letter he writes "I am almost eighty". The year usually given for his death is 1691. The file we have does not state a year, so treat that date as coming from outside the book.
The book

Lawrence did not write this as a book. The title page calls it "Conversations and Letters", and that is what it is. There are four Conversations, which are another person's notes of what he said, and fifteen Letters, which the edition presents as his own, to correspondents the book mostly does not name. Most notes in the Conversations begin with the word "That", because they are reported speech, a continuation of "He told me that". We call the person who took them the note-taker. The preface says the Conversations are "supposed to have been written by M. Beaufort", a Grand Vicar, an official who helps a bishop run his diocese.
A note in the edition, on the last letter, records that he took to his bed two days later and died within the week. So the book as we have it was put together by others, after his death.

One more detail. A stretch at the end of the Fourth Conversation carries a footnote saying that its particulars are collected from other accounts of him. Every passage in this book comes from the four Conversations and the Letters, never from that stretch or from the preface. (This chapter does quote the preface and the title page, and says so each time.)
Why it suits a pilgrim

It is not a book about a destination. It is a book about how to go about a day: how to begin, what to do when your mind runs off, how to do a task you dislike, what to make of a flat hour. It comes in short pieces, which is how a walker reads, and it is a book of attention, which a road tends to ask for whether or not you offer it.

The unsigned preface, which speaks for the edition and not for Lawrence, says he "lived his Christian life through as a pilgrim" and "as a steward and not as an owner". The title page calls the publisher "Publishers of Evangelical Literature", so a Catholic lay brother is presented by an evangelical house. Read the preface's blessings and comments as the edition's, not his.

It is also a hard book in places, and a seventeenth-century one. He calls himself wretched, often. From the Eleventh Letter on he writes of sickness and pain as gifts from God, which is hard to read when you are in pain, and we have not tried to defend or explain it. All of that is left out. We chose the passages that speak most plainly to someone on a road.
The translation, the edition and the licence

The English in the passages comes from an old print edition, "Translated from the French" as its title page says. The file names no translator and prints no year, so under each passage we credit an anonymous translation from the French, Fleming H. Revell Company edition (the company of New York, Chicago and Toronto), and we do not guess a date. It is on Project Gutenberg as ebook number 13871, and every quotation here was checked against that text, word for word.

We treat the translation as public domain. Lawrence died in the seventeenth century, and the edition is an old print with no modern editor named and no modern copyright notice in the file. Project Gutenberg offers it as a print edition not protected by United States copyright. For other countries we can say no more than that the translation is old and anonymous.

We changed nothing in the passages. We kept the old spellings, the capital letters the print uses for GOD and LORD (the old way of setting the divine names, not shouting), and the "That" at the head of a note. We left out the small footnote numbers. Where we skip a stretch inside a passage, a mark like this shows it: …. The choice of the six passages, their order, the reflections, the questions and the prayers are ours and they are original. Four of the six passages come from the Letters and two from the Conversations, one of those drawing on two.
None of the Project Gutenberg licence text or trademark is copied into this book.
What is the least you need to set out in good company?
The passage

paras.t: He requires no great matters of us; a little remembrance of Him from time to time; a little adoration; sometimes to pray for His grace, sometimes to offer Him your sufferings, and sometimes to return Him thanks for the favors He has given you, and still gives you, in the midst of your troubles, and to console yourself with Him the oftenest you can. Lift up your heart to Him, sometimes even at your meals, and when you are in company: the least little remembrance will always be acceptable to Him. You need not cry very loud; He is nearer to us than we are aware of. … Every one is capable of such familiar conversation with GOD, some more, some less: He knows what we can do. Let us begin, then. Perhaps He expects but one generous resolution on our part. Have courage.

cite.t: The Practice of the Presence of God
, Seventh Letter (anonymous translation from the French, Fleming H. Revell Company edition)

spans.t: Reflection

On the first morning the list in your head is probably long. Water, the charger, tape for the heel, whether the shoes will do, whether the first day is too long or too short. A pack that was sorted last night gets sorted again at the door. There is nothing wrong with that. A road is a lot to begin, and a list is how the mind holds a lot.

Brother Lawrence has a list too, and it is shorter than any you will write today. It comes from a letter to someone the book does not name, someone who seems to be in trouble, since the letter opens with "I pity you much." And it begins with what is not being asked. The "He" of the passage is God, whose name this old print sets in capitals. God, says the letter, "requires no great matters of us". A little remembrance now and then. A little adoration, which you may read as a moment of plain wonder or thanks. A word asked for, an ache offered, a thank-you, a bit of comfort taken. Lift up your heart, he says, even at a meal, even in company. There is no need to shout. God is nearer than we know.

Notice the verbs in that list: to ask, to offer, to thank. You will probably do all three before lunch without calling them anything. You ask the hill to end. You put up with a heel. You are grateful for a patch of shade. Lawrence only suggests that these small movements of the heart have somewhere to go, and that going there takes no more than a moment.

Then, after a line we will come back to, comes a sentence that is kind to everybody. Every one is capable of this familiar conversation, "some more, some less". The letter does not say how much. It says only that God knows what we can do, and then it says the best thing a letter can say to a person on a doorstep:
let us begin, then.
This suits a first day for two reasons.

The first is scale. The first day of a road is when resolutions are biggest. You will walk every step in silence. You will stop at every church. You will give up the phone. By the third day a resolution of that size has met a blister. A resolution of the size Lawrence asks, one small remembrance, now and then, can survive a blister, not because it is easy but because there is so little of it to break.
The second is place. The lines hidden by the ellipsis say that to be with God you need not always be at church. You may make a small chapel of your heart, a word he gives in its old form, an
oratory

, and slip into it from time to time. On a road that passes churches which may be shut, and long stretches that pass none at all, that thought travels well. The chapel is not a building you reach by evening. You carry it.

Where is it hard? At the very first word. "Him" is God, and Lawrence is not offering a way to feel calm. He is describing a friendship with someone he is sure is there. If you are not sure, or are sure of the opposite, you can read this as a stranger's kind letter and keep what fits: the smallness, the permission to begin badly, the idea that attention is something you can give a little at a time. Do that knowing it is a borrowing.

It is hard, too, that the letter offers no cure. "In the midst of your troubles" is as far as it goes. The remembrance is company in the trouble, not a door out of it. Anyone who has carried something heavy onto a road will know the difference, and may find the plainness of it a relief.

And there is the age of the writer. A little further on in the same letter he says "I am almost eighty". A man of that age may well have stopped waiting for the right moment to start, and the shortness of his advice suggests it.

What does it ask of an ordinary day? Very little, and that is the point. One remembrance in the first hour. Another when you sit down for water or coffee. Do not count them, do not grade them. Let them be late, and plain, and a little clumsy. A remembrance is not a performance. If it takes one breath, it is finished.
For the walk

items.t: What is the first place today where I could stop for the length of one breath?

When you first sit down, before you reach for the phone or the food, stay still for one breath and say, quietly or silently, "Here I am." Say it to God if that is your word. If it is not, say it to the morning, or to yourself, or to whoever is nearest. Then go on. The shorter it is, the better it keeps. If you forget until noon, do it at noon.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Boots off. Whatever kind of day it was, the evening is when your feet make their report, and they should be heard first, before any other part of you has an opinion. Sit for a minute with them. Drink some water, eat something, see to whatever needs seeing to. The rest of this can wait ten minutes. It will not be offended.

The first evening of a road can feel like a verdict on the whole plan: too tired, too far, too much. It is not a verdict. A first day is mostly your body finding out what you have asked of it, and it will have a good deal to say.

Now look back over the day with the letter in mind. How many little remembrances were there? If the honest answer is none, that is a fair first count and nothing to be ashamed of. You set out with a list, a pack and a body to look after, and a day on foot is very full of the next thing. If the answer is one or two, a pause on a bench, a moment when you noticed the light and were glad to be here, then keep those. They are the whole of what the letter asks.

Think also about what you carried that you did not need. Some of it was in the pack, and you may find out tonight by lifting it. Some of it was in your head: a worry about the days to come, a plan for the whole road, a comparison with how other people seem to be doing. Lawrence's list is short because he had put down most of the other one. You do not have to put yours down tonight. You only have to see what is on it.

And remember why you came. People set out for all sorts of reasons: a promise, a grief, a question, a rest, a curiosity that would not go away. Reasons get buried under logistics by the second hour, under water and weather and where to sleep. The evening is a fair time to dig yours out and see that it is still there. It does not need to be a grand one. "I wanted to see if I could" is a complete reason, and so is "I did not know what else to do."

If there is someone at home on your mind tonight, you could offer them a remembrance too, as small as the letter's: one kind sentence, said inwardly, with no message sent. It costs nothing, and it keeps them company.
If the God of the letter is a question for you, tonight is not the time to answer it. Be tired in peace. One plain sentence will do:
I was here today.
The questions for tonight:

items.t: When, even for a moment, did I notice that I was glad to be on this road?
What did I carry today, in the pack or in my head, that I did not need?
Where could one small pause fit into tomorrow morning?

spans.t: A short prayer

For the road behind me, thank you. For the road ahead, be near. I asked for no great matter today and I ask for none tonight. Keep my feet. Keep my small resolution. Let me sleep, and begin again in the morning.
What if the job you least want is where the day is actually lived?
The passage

paras.t: That he had been lately sent into Burgundy, to buy the provision of wine for the society, which was a very unwelcome task for him, because he had no turn for business, and because he was lame and could not go about the boat but by rolling himself over the casks. That however he gave himself no uneasiness about it, nor about the purchase of the wine. That he said to GOD,
It was His business he was about

, and that he afterwards found it very well performed. … So, likewise, in his business in the kitchen (to which he had naturally a great aversion), having accustomed himself to do everything there for the love of GOD, and with prayer, upon all occasions, for His grace to do his work well, he had found everything easy, during fifteen years that he had been employed there.

cite.t: The Practice of the Presence of God
, Second Conversation (anonymous translation from the French, Fleming H. Revell Company edition)

spans.t: Reflection

A road is mostly chores. Nobody puts that on the postcard. There is the pack to repack, the water to find and fill, the socks to wash in a sink and wring out, the heel to see to, the bed to make up from a sleeping bag or a sheet. There is the long middle of the afternoon, which has to be walked whether or not you feel like walking it. The lovely parts are the minority, and the chores are what is left when the lovely parts have gone by.

Brother Lawrence had chores too, and by the account we have, he did not choose them. The notes of the Second Conversation say that he had been sent to Burgundy to buy the community's wine, and that he found it a very unwelcome task. He had no head for business. He was lame, and the only way he could get about the boat was by rolling himself over the casks. (The notes are in the third person, as if reported to someone else, and the "society" is his religious community.)
Then comes what he did about it, as the note-taker has it. He gave himself no uneasiness, and he told God that it was His business he was about.

Look at how small that move is. The word "business" turns up for two different things here: the trade he had no head for, and the errand that was God's. It would be a neat joke if it were meant as one, and it is a neat idea even if it was not.

The casks are still there. He is still lame. The wine still has to be bought, and he does not claim to have found a talent he lacked. The notes say it went well, and they are the only evidence we have. What changed is not the job. It is whose errand it is. Not "my wretched duty" but "His business". And an errand that belongs to someone else loses much of what makes a dull errand heavy: the commentary about whether you are good at it, whether it is fair, whether it is beneath you.

The kitchen is the same lesson at a slower speed. He had, the passage says, "naturally a great aversion" to it. He did not come to love it, or at least that is not what the notes claim. What they say is that he did everything there for the love of God, asked for grace to do it well, and found everything easy, in the fifteen years he had been at it. Easy is not the same as liked. You can find a thing easy and still not care for it, the way a road gets easier once you stop arguing with it.
There are three places where this is hard.

The first is the word "easy". It sounds too good, and it is a report from fifteen years in. It says nothing about the first week, or the first month, or about the man he was before, who in the First Conversation calls himself "a great awkward fellow who broke everything". Do not hold your own first week to a standard set by someone's fifteenth year.

The second is that handing a task over does not take the ache out of it. Your feet will still hurt. Lawrence is not saying that a heavy pack becomes light, or that a hated job becomes a pleasure. He is saying that a thing can be done whole instead of grudgingly, and that the difference matters even when the thing is no easier.

The third is the phrase "His business". It helps if God is the one you mean. If that is more than you can honestly say, there is a plainer version nearby: the errand in front of you is simply the thing you are doing, and you have only this one chance to do it. The grumbling about it, and the planning of better errands elsewhere, are a second job nobody asked you to take. Putting that second job down is most of what he is describing.

So what does it ask of an ordinary afternoon on a road? Take one chore, the dullest on offer, and do it all the way through. Not as a lesson, not for the sake of becoming a better person. Because it is the part of the day you would otherwise spend somewhere else, and the day has only so many hours. There is a quiet pleasure waiting at the far end, too: the moment a chore is finished and does not need doing again.
For the walk

items.t: Which part of today am I only trying to get through?

When the dullest task comes up (the laces, the repack, the queue, the refilling of the bottle), do it as if it were the only thing in the day. Slowly, with both hands and your whole attention. When it is finished, say "done" to yourself, and let it go. If you cannot decide which chore to choose, take the first one that turns up. It will do.

spans.t: At the end of the day

If the place you are staying has a sink, it is probably busy. Socks, a shirt, the second shirt, something you do not want to look at too closely. Hands in cold water, soap of uncertain purpose, a wringing that squeezes out half of what it should. It is a very small chore. It is also, if you let it be, a good place to think about the passage.

Go back over the day and find the part you fought. There will be one. It might have been a stretch of road with nothing to look at, a hill that arrived at the wrong time, the daily business of packing, or a conversation you did not want. Ask what the fighting cost. Often it costs more than the thing itself: the hill took an hour, and the argument with the hill took the hour and the morning.

Then look for the opposite, however brief. Was there a moment in the day when you did one thing with all of yourself? Not necessarily a good thing. Tying a lace, pouring water, closing a gate, looking properly at a village. If you cannot find one, that is information, not failure, and tomorrow offers plenty of chances. Nobody learns to say "His business" by tomorrow lunchtime.

There is a small pleasure in a finished chore that is easy to overlook. The sock is on the line, the bottle is full, the pack is closed. These "done" moments are the real milestones of a day on foot, and they come far more often than the kilometres do.

The evening has its own errands, and they are the same kind: wash, hang, eat, charge the phone, lay out tomorrow's clothes. They are not in the way of the rest. They are the rest, taken one small job at a time.

It is worth noticing the chores that were not a fight. The first drink of the day that tasted of something. Unlacing the boots. Hot water on tired feet, if you had it. Nobody offers a prize for these, and they are some of the best minutes a day on foot can give. There is a tiredness that comes from the fight and a tiredness that comes from the work, and tonight you may be able to tell them apart. The second is the cleaner of the two.

Is there a chore you have been putting off since the first morning? The heel you have not looked at properly, the message you have not answered, the bag you keep meaning to sort. Name it tonight. Naming it costs nothing, and it is half of doing it.

Be gentle about tonight. This is not the evening to optimise anything. If the washing will not dry, it will dry on the pack. If the chores are not finished, they will be there in the morning, and they will be exactly the same size.
The questions for tonight:

items.t: Which task today did I try to get through instead of being in it?
Was there a moment, however short, when I did one thing with all of myself?
What chore will tomorrow bring, and how could I meet it without a fight?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for the plain work of this day. For the pack and the water and the wet socks, for the miles I only put up with. Let tomorrow's errands be Yours, and let me be in them. Give my hands something to do and my mind something to rest on. Good night.
When your mind has run off, how do you walk back?
The passage

paras.t: You tell me nothing new; you are not the only one that is troubled with wandering thoughts. Our mind is extremely roving; but, as the will is mistress of all our faculties, she must recall them, and carry them to GOD as their last end. … Let it be

business to keep your mind in the presence of the LORD. If it sometimes wander and withdraw itself from Him, do not much disquiet yourself for that: trouble and disquiet serve rather to distract the mind than to re-collect it: the will must bring it back in tranquility.

cite.t: The Practice of the Presence of God
, Eighth Letter (anonymous translation from the French, Fleming H. Revell Company edition)

spans.t: Reflection

At some point today you may well walk past a turn. The waymark was there, a yellow arrow on a wall or a post, and you were somewhere else: inside an argument from last spring, or composing a reply you will never send, or deciding what to eat. A few hundred metres on, something is off. The path has no arrows. You stop. You turn round. Nothing is lost but ten minutes and a small amount of dignity, and you walk back to the place where you stopped paying attention.

The mind does this all day, and Lawrence knew it well. The edition we use heads this letter with a note, "Concerning wandering thoughts in Prayer", and the letter itself is a reply to someone who has confessed to the problem. Look at how it begins. "You tell me nothing new." Is there a kinder way to meet a person who is ashamed? He does not sigh, or quote a rule. He says: you are not the only one. The mind roves, and it roves in everybody.

Then he gives what we would call his method, and it is gentler than the word suggests. The will, he says, is "mistress of all our faculties", and "she" must recall them and carry them to God as their "last end", the place everything is meant to arrive. For Lawrence that is God; for a walker it can be as plain as where you are going today. (In his day the faculties were the powers of the mind, such as memory and understanding, and the will was the part of you that chooses.) The picture is of a person calling back a flock, not of a guard with a stick. And notice that the calling is done "in tranquility". The last sentence of the passage is the one worth underlining: "trouble and disquiet serve rather to distract the mind than to re-collect it."

In plain words: the scolding is a second wandering. When you find that you have drifted, the drift is not the thing that takes you furthest from where you meant to be. The self-reproach is. It adds a lap of the same field.

The phone is a very efficient wanderer. It can take your mind to eleven places before the next village. This is not a sermon about phones. Lawrence had none, and his mind roved like anyone's. The phone only makes the roving easier to do and harder to notice.

He did not preach this from a height. In the Second Conversation the note-taker reports that at the beginning he often spent the time set aside for prayer "rejecting wandering thoughts, and falling back into them." A man whose whole book is about attention spent whole sittings failing at it. In the Third Conversation he is said to have gone a good while without thinking of God and not to have disquieted himself, but to have owned up and returned, "with so much the greater trust in Him". The return is not a penalty. It is the practice itself.
It is hard in two places.

The first is the sentence "the will must bring it back". Some days it cannot. The mind is held by something heavy: grief, an illness at home, a dread about what is waiting when the road ends. Then the wandering is not a lapse. It is weather. On those days the passage is not an instruction, only a permission: do not add reproach to a weight you are already carrying.

The second is that not all wandering is waste. Lawrence is speaking of one particular practice, keeping his mind in God's presence, and the passage does not tell you to stop thinking about your life. On a long walk a good deal of what the mind does is sorting and remembering and rehearsing, and that may be the very work you came out to do. A walking mind is allowed to walk. What the passage offers is a way back for the moments when you wanted to be somewhere and were not. You are the only one who can tell which moments those are.

One more word, since the letter is about God: "the presence of the LORD" is the place Lawrence wants his mind to return to. If that place is not one you can name, the turn still works at its simplest. You come back to the road under your feet, which is also a place, and is also always there.
What does it ask of an ordinary day? That you treat each return as a small success and not a small defeat. The arrow was missed, the arrow was found. The finding is the walking.
For the walk

items.t: Where did my mind go in the last ten minutes, and can I bring it back without a word of blame?

Whenever you notice you have drifted, to the phone, a worry, a tune that will not stop, let the noticing count as a success. Touch the strap of your pack or take one slow breath, and come back to the path. Count the returns, not the drifts. If it helps, give each return a one-word name, such as "back". By evening you may have more than you expect. If you lose count, that is only another drift, and you know what to do with those.

spans.t: At the end of the day

By evening the mind is as tired as the legs, and it wanders further. That is worth knowing before you grade yourself. A mind at nine at night is not the mind that set out at eight, and it would be unfair to ask the same of it.

Think back over where it went today. Some of the places will be forgettable: a stretch of road spent with a stuck song, a long argument with a person who was not there. Others will have been returned to, over and over, like a tongue to a sore tooth. A particular worry. A particular face. If there was something your mind kept going back to, it may not have been a distraction at all. It may have been trying to tell you something you did not have time to hear while you were walking. Tonight, with the light low and nothing to do, you could give it a minute of the attention it was asking for. Not a solution. Only a hearing.
Then think about how you spoke to yourself when you noticed you had strayed. There is a tone people take with their own minds that they would never take with a friend:
there you go again.
Lawrence offers another.
You are not the only one.
If you can hear the second voice, even faintly, try saying it once, to yourself, as you would to someone you were fond of.

And what helped you come back? It is useful to know. For some people it is a sound, a bell or a dog or the scrape of a stick. For some it is a step that landed badly. For some it is a person who said good morning. The things that call us back are often small and often outside us, and a road is full of them. You may find that you have a few that work for you.

The same letter has an image for the end of a day like this, and it may fit better than any advice. Lawrence tells his reader to hold themselves before God "like a dumb or paralytic beggar at a rich man's gate". ("Dumb" in his English means unable to speak.) A person who cannot speak and cannot move can do nothing but be there, and being there is, as we read him, the whole of the business. If you have no words tonight and no energy, you are well placed. You may be nearer to the gate than you were at noon.
If sleep will not come and the mind is running, do not fight it. Treat each time you notice as a return. You are practising in the dark, and it counts as much as it did at noon.
Do not sit up long with this. A tired mind will not sort itself out in the dark, and there is a lot to be said for sleeping on it.
The questions for tonight:

items.t: Where did my mind keep going today, and what was it asking for?
How did I speak to myself when I noticed I had drifted?
What helped me come back: a sound, a step, a person, a breath?

spans.t: A short prayer

I wandered today, and here I am. No speeches. Take what was scattered and gather it gently. Let me be as patient with my mind as You are. Tomorrow I will lose the way again, and again find it. Stay near.
What do you do on the day when nothing is felt?
The passage

paras.t: I do not say that therefore we must put any violent constraint upon ourselves. No, we must serve GOD in a holy freedom; we must do our business faithfully; without trouble or disquiet, recalling our mind to GOD mildly, and with tranquility, as often as we find it wandering from Him. … Be not discouraged by the repugnance which you may find in it from nature; you must do yourself violence. At the first one often thinks it lost time, but you must go on, and resolve to persevere in it to death, notwithstanding all the difficulties that may occur.

cite.t: The Practice of the Presence of God
, Sixth Letter (anonymous translation from the French, Fleming H. Revell Company edition)

spans.t: Reflection

Sooner or later there is a stretch where nothing happens. The path runs straight, or the village you were counting on is shut, or the weather is the colour of dishwater. The excitement of the first morning has worn off, and the end is still too far away to taste. You are walking, and you feel precisely nothing. Not bored, even. Flat. A voice that sounds like your own asks what exactly you think you are doing here.
On a road of about a week this is roughly where the middle falls, though it may arrive on any day, and it comes whether or not the scenery is good. This is the day for Lawrence's Sixth Letter.

Read the passage twice and you will find two moods in it. The first is gentle. There is to be no "violent constraint". We are to serve God "in a holy freedom", do our work faithfully, and call the wandering mind home "mildly, and with tranquility". The second is firm. Do not be discouraged by the reluctance you find in yourself. "At the first one often thinks it lost time, but you must go on."

The two sit side by side in the same letter, and he does not stop to reconcile them. A fair reading is that he is gentle about how and firm about whether. You do not whip yourself. You also do not stop because the feeling has stopped. Everything he writes assumes that the practice will, for long stretches, seem pointless, and that the pointless-seeming hours are part of it and not a sign that it has failed.

Notice, too, "we must do our business faithfully". Business again, as on the second day: the plain work in front of you. On a road the business is walking, and it can be done faithfully on a day when it is done without a feeling.

The word worth stopping at is "lost". Lost against what? Against a measure: a feeling, a result, a picture of how the practice ought to be going. The hours seem lost because the measure is not being met. Read that way, "go on" means keep walking, and let the measure go quiet.

He is not speaking from a place of ease. In the Second Letter he says, "for the first ten years I suffered much", and in the First Conversation, the note-taker has him telling of "dryness, or insensibilities and irksomenesses" in prayer, a gift of a word for the grey hours of a long afternoon. A man who tells you that the beginning is hard is not selling you a feeling. He is telling you what the middle looks like from the inside, and that it is survivable.
There are two places where this passage needs care, and one of them is about your body.

The first is the phrase "you must do yourself violence". It is not one we would choose today, and it should not be read as an order to push through pain. "Go on" is about the practice, the small returning of the attention, and about the feeling that it is a waste of time. It is not about your knee. If a foot, a joint, a head or a chest is telling you something that worries you, stop. Rest. Ask someone. See a doctor if it does not settle. If it is an emergency in Spain, the number is 112. Nothing in this passage asks you to walk on an injury for the sake of a mood.

The second place is the feeling itself. Sometimes "lost time" is a true report. The day may be flat because you are depleted, or underfed, or in need of a rest day, or because the road has stopped being the right thing for now. The passage is about the particular dullness of a practice that is working in the dark. It does not forbid you to notice that a day is simply a bad one, and to treat it kindly.

He also, in the First Conversation, reads such hours as ways "by which GOD tries our love to him". That is a claim about God's purposes, and it will land differently on different readers. You do not have to accept it to take the sense of it: that a flat hour is not the same as a wasted one, and that what you do inside it still counts.

So what does it ask of a flat afternoon? Not enthusiasm. Only the next small thing, done gently. One foot, then another. A look at what is actually in front of you. And no verdict on the hour until it is over.
For the walk

items.t: What can I do with an hour in which I feel nothing?

When the thought "this is lost time" turns up, pick a fixed thing ahead of you, a post, a gate, a bend, a tree, and walk to it without any commentary. Then pick another. Keep to an ordinary pace, and do not try to cure the flatness by hurrying. Do not judge the hour until the evening. If it helps, make the hour smaller: not "until the next village" but "until that gate". Ask nothing more of the afternoon than the gate, and eat something while you are at it.

spans.t: At the end of the day
A flat day is hard to describe at the end of it, because nothing happened. There is no scene to tell. Just a lot of time, and your feet at the bottom of it.

Check the body before anything else. A flat afternoon is sometimes only a body asking for food, water, salt, sleep, or a sit-down it has been refused for hours. If you have not eaten properly, eat. If you have not drunk, drink. The feeling of futility can be astonishingly sensitive to a sandwich. This is not a trick. It is a reminder that you are an animal as well as a pilgrim, and the animal has views.

Then look at the grey stretch. When did it start? Often it has an edge: a hill, a lunch missed, a bad night, an unwanted message. When did it ease, if it did? Sometimes a flat spell ends so quietly that you could not say when. You look up and the light has changed and you are walking differently. It is worth noticing whether that happened, and what you were doing when it did. If it did not ease, and you are still in it tonight, that is allowed. Lawrence's ten years were not a week. A single day of greyness is nothing to be afraid of.
The passage says "persevere in it to death", and by that Lawrence means for life, not for the next week. Tonight you need only persevere until morning.

Make a short list in your head of three small things that were fine today. Not good, only fine: a wall with the sun on it, a nod from a stranger, the moment the stone came out of the shoe. Flat days carry small good things, and they are easy to miss because you were looking for large ones. Fine is underrated. A week is built mostly of it.

Some of the people around you tonight may have had the same afternoon. Nobody announces it. There is a quiet company in a room of people who have each been through a flat day and are not going to mention it.

And ask whether the time was truly lost. Think of what you did anyway. A kilometre walked without joy is still a kilometre. A courtesy offered in a flat mood is as real as one offered in a glad one, and perhaps costs a little more. If you cannot find anything, then you did what some days are for. You went on.
If anything hurt today in a way that surprised you, look at it now, in good light, and decide about tomorrow. A rest day is an ordinary part of a road, and so is asking someone for help.
Then rest, properly, without making it another task. Lawrence's two moods apply here as well: be gentle about how, and firm about whether. Tonight that means sleeping.
The questions for tonight:

items.t: Where today did I think "this is lost time", and what did I do with the thought?
What did I do anyway that I am quietly glad of?
What does my body need tonight, and have I given it?

spans.t: A short prayer
Nothing to report. The road was long and I felt little. Be with me in the flat hours as You are in the bright ones. I will not pretend. Let me go on gently, and rest well, and wake without a verdict.

chapters.title: Day 5. A straw from the ground

spans.t: What small thing are you about to walk past?
The passage

paras.t: That he was pleased when he could take up a straw from the ground for the love of GOD, seeking Him only, and nothing else, not even His gifts. … That we ought not to be weary of doing little things for the love of GOD, who regards not the greatness of the work, but the love with which it is performed.

cite.t: The Practice of the Presence of God
, Second and Fourth Conversations (anonymous translation from the French, Fleming H. Revell Company edition)

spans.t: Reflection

There is something at the side of every path. A glove that fell out of a pocket. A gate that was left open behind somebody. A strap that has twisted on another walker's pack, which they cannot reach. A plastic straw in the verge, bleached by the weather. A person looking at their feet. At walking pace you pass dozens of these in a morning, and walking pace is fast enough to miss every one.

Brother Lawrence's example is the smallest object he could have chosen. The notes of the Second Conversation say he was pleased when he could pick up a straw from the ground for the love of God. Not a rescue, not a sacrifice. A straw. In our day the straw is more likely to be plastic, and the verge is where you will find it.

The second half of the passage, from the Fourth Conversation, supplies the principle. God, he says, "regards not the greatness of the work, but the love with which it is performed." In plain words: nobody is keeping a scale of large and small. A thing done with care is the size of the care.

That matters more on a road than it might at home, because nearly everything you are given on a road is small: a plaster, a pointing hand, a word of warning about the next hill. Nearly everything you give will be small too. If small things count for nothing, almost all of what passes between walkers is wasted. By Lawrence's account they count for exactly what the love in them is worth.

There is a kind of freedom in the example he chose. Nobody could be proud of picking up a straw. A deed that small cannot be a boast, and a deed too small to be noticed is hard to do for the sake of being noticed.

Be honest about what this passage is and is not. Lawrence's examples are a straw, a kitchen, a cask of wine. He does not, in these lines, tell his reader to be kind to the people on the road. That step from the straw to the neighbour is ours, and it is a short one. In the Ninth Letter he does write that "we ought to help one another by our advice, and yet more by our good examples", and near its close the Fifteenth Letter says, "Let us pray for one another." What the passage gives you is the shape of an act, small, attentive and unadvertised, and the road offers a good many people to practise it on.

The harder half is the straw's, and it hides in the last words of that sentence: "seeking Him only, and nothing else, not even His gifts". The sense seems to be that he did not do the small thing for the glow. His "gifts" appear to mean the sweetness and consolation that can come with prayer. He did the small thing for no reward at all, including that one. Put into walking terms: the kindness that is waiting for the other person's face to light up, or for the thank-you, or for the tidy warm sensation of being a good pilgrim, is not quite what he describes. That is a high bar, and most of us will not clear it by lunchtime. It is still worth knowing where the bar is.
There are two more difficulties.

One is that small kindness can be a performance. A road is full of people, and it is easy to find yourself being a helpful walker in front of an audience. The check is simple, if uncomfortable: would you still do it if no one at all could see? The closed gate, the carried rubbish, the greeting to the person who will not look up. Those are the straw. The lent charger announced to the whole room is something else.

The other is that small things can be a way of avoiding a large one. Picking up straws is a comfortable occupation. If there is a call that should be made, an apology that is owed, a decision waiting at the end of the road, a morning of kindly tidying will not discharge it. The passage does not say otherwise. It speaks of little things as worth doing well, not as a way round the day's larger business.

What does it ask of an ordinary stretch of path? To look up from the middle distance. To notice the one small thing within reach, and to do it, once, without a word. If it is a dropped glove and its owner is out of earshot, the glove can be set on a wall or a post at eye height, where they may look if they come back. That is the whole of the act. Then to carry on, a little lighter, and not tell anyone, including yourself.
For the walk

items.t: What small thing am I about to walk past?
Do one small thing today that no one will see or thank you for. Close a gate. Carry a bit of rubbish to the next bin. Say
Buen Camino

to someone who is watching their feet. Then do not mention it, to anyone, or in your own head afterwards. Let it stay where you left it, like the straw. It may feel slightly foolish. That is a good sign, since it means the thing was small. If nothing offers itself, look for the second thing. And if someone does something small for you, let them, and say thank you.

spans.t: At the end of the day

Kindness is one of the first things to go at the end of a long day. By the time the bed is found and the boots are off, there is often very little left in the tank for strangers, and the person asking if the other bunk is taken can receive a shorter answer than they deserved. If that was you, it was not a character flaw. It was a long day of walking.

Start with what you were given. A direction offered without being asked. A bit of tape, or a plaster. A seat shifted along a bench. Someone holding a door, or pointing out a puddle. These things arrive so lightly that they are easy to receive without noticing, and the day goes by with a good deal of unpaid thanks outstanding. If you can remember one, you could say thank you to it now, in your head, to a face you may not see again. It is a small payment and it goes a long way.

Think, too, of what you used today without knowing who made it possible. The path under your feet. The arrow that kept you right. The bed you are lying in, with its blanket and its pillow. Someone made each of those, or mended them, or kept them going, and you will probably never meet them. A road is built, all the way along, out of small acts by people who are not there. It might be good to be glad of them for a moment.

Then what did you pass? Think of the straws that were at the edge of your day. Not to scold yourself, only to find out what stopped you. Sometimes it was hurry, and sometimes it was shyness. Sometimes it was a plain fatigue that left nothing to give, and that deserves the same tenderness as anything else. Often it was only that you did not see. Seeing is a skill, and it gets better with use.

Lawrence's "not even His gifts" can be a quiet evening question. Was there a moment today when you did something kind and noticed that you were waiting for it to be returned? You do not need to answer. It is enough to be able to notice.

Receiving is a kindness too. A person who lets you help them, or who takes the offered plaster without a speech, has given you something, and it is worth remembering that you can give it back by receiving well.
If the day left you nothing to give, then nothing was owed. Some days you are the person being carried, and that is as much a part of a road as the carrying.
Then, if you are up to it, set one small act for the morning, and tell nobody. Not a grand intention. A straw. If the morning gets in the way, it will keep.
The questions for tonight:

items.t: What small kindness did I receive today without saying thank you?
Was there something small I passed by, and what stopped me?
What is one thing I could do tomorrow that no one will see?

spans.t: A short prayer

For the small kindnesses I was given and did not notice, thank you. For the ones I passed by, forgive me. Make my hands quick and my attention kind. Let me do one little thing well tomorrow, and not need to be thanked. Rest.
What is worth carrying home?
The passage

paras.t: How can we pray to Him without being with Him? How can we be with Him but in thinking of Him often? And how can we often think of Him, but by a holy habit which we should form of it? You will tell me that I am always saying the same thing. It is true, for this is the best and easiest method I know; and as I use no other, I advise all the world to do it.

cite.t: The Practice of the Presence of God
, Ninth Letter (anonymous translation from the French, Fleming H. Revell Company edition)

spans.t: Reflection

The last stretch of a road is the one you can least picture. You will have pictured the arrival, perhaps: the long approach, the first sight of the city, the end. It is much harder to picture the feeling of it, which may be a mixture of relief and a small, strange loss. A body that has spent days on its feet does not know what to do with a stopped afternoon. A mind that has been given a single task, to get to the next place, finds itself without one.
Which brings us to the question the last day has to carry. What now? And what, if anything, of this goes home?

Lawrence's answer, in the Ninth Letter, is almost comically plain. He builds a little staircase of questions. How can we pray to God without being with God? How can we be with God but by thinking of Him often? How can we think of Him often, but by forming a habit? Then, before anyone can say it, he says it for them: "You will tell me that I am always saying the same thing." And he agrees. It is true. It is the best and easiest method he knows, and he uses no other.

Take the first word out of the staircase and it still stands, which is worth seeing. How can you attend to anything without being with it? How can you be with it without thinking of it often? How can you think of it often except by habit? That is our paraphrase, not his, and it is not what he means. He means God. But it shows how little the shape depends on the name, for a reader who is not ready to use it.

There is something endearing in an old man admitting that he has only one tune. And there is a lot of sense in it. The six days of this book have been the same thing said in six kinds of weather. A little remembrance, on the first morning. The same remembrance inside a chore. The same turning back, after the mind has run off. The same going on, when nothing could be felt. The same attention, spent on a straw. And today, the habit that holds them together. If you have kept anything at all, it is probably only one of these, and it is probably the one that was easiest to repeat.

A road is the same thing again, too. You do not walk a whole road. You walk one step, and then one step, and the road is only what that comes to. Lawrence's method is the same arithmetic applied to attention: a small turning, over and over, until it is less of an effort than not turning. In the Fourth Conversation the note-taker has him saying that "we should not wonder if, in the beginning, we often failed in our endeavors", and that in time "we should gain a habit". Habit is the bridge between the road and the rest of your life.

At the front of the same letter there is a line to hold on to as well. He writes of someone who "would go faster than grace", and adds that one does not become holy all at once. You could say it of a walker who sets out too fast, or of a reader who tries to keep too much. One of the things the road teaches, if you let it, is the pace at which a person can actually go on.
There are three honest difficulties.

The first is "the best and easiest". Easiest to describe, perhaps. Day 4 of this book knew better: it is not an easy practice to keep when nothing comes of it, and in the Fourteenth Letter he says himself that "the beginning is very difficult". Take the word as his enthusiasm, not as a promise.

The second is "I advise all the world to do it." This book does not. It offers one man's way of keeping company with God to anyone who would like to try it, and it is content if you take a single line and leave the rest. In this letter Lawrence is a Christian writing to a fellow member of a religious community, and he is not writing to us. What a reader of another faith, or none, does with his advice is their own affair.

The third is the difference between a road and home. A road holds you. The arrows are painted, the day has a direction, other people are walking the same way, and the whole of your attention is permitted to be on one thing. Home has none of that. A habit that was easy on the road may feel absurd beside a kettle on a wet morning. Be ready for it to fade a little in the second week. Be ready to begin again, which is, after all, the same thing again.
What does it ask of an ordinary day? Only that you choose one. And hang it on something you already do, so that you do not need to remember it.
For the walk

items.t: What is the one thing from these six days I would be glad to still be doing in a month?

Choose a place you pass every day at home, a doorway, a kettle, a bus stop, a step, and decide that it will be your bench. Whenever you reach it, stop for one breath. If you are still on the road as you read this, walk the last quarter of an hour in silence, and let the last thing you notice be the first thing you take home.

spans.t: At the end of the day
Tonight can be quiet. Not every ending needs a ceremony, and some of the best ones are no more than a person sitting on the edge of a bed with the light off, saying nothing in particular.

If the road has ended for you, or ends tomorrow, you may feel a little flat, and that is no surprise. A purpose that has filled days does not leave without a gap. The body will need a few days to believe it can stop. Do not ask yourself tonight to say what it all meant. A walk of this kind is not a thing that can be summed up on the evening it finishes, and most of what it has done will not show for a while.

Think back over the six days instead of over the one. Was there a morning on which something small turned up that you would have walked past on the first day? Was there a moment that surprised you with its quiet? No conclusion is required. A list will do: the things that stayed.

If you walked beside people for a day or two and are about to part, a goodbye said properly is a small kindness, the same size as the straw. You may never see them again. A name, a handshake, a "thank you for the company" costs a minute and is remembered longer than the conversation.

Then ask which of the six you would most like to read again. It does not have to be the best one. It can be the one that stuck in your teeth. A book of this kind is better read twice, and a passage that annoyed you the first time is often the one with something in it.

And think of the place at home that you chose for your breath. Picture it, the doorway or the bus stop, and picture yourself stopping there. Not a speech, only a pause. If the picture makes you smile, that is a good sign. If it makes you wince, choose a gentler place.

Tomorrow, if you are not walking, there may be a strange morning in which the body wakes at its road hour and finds nothing to do. Let it. Decide in advance that you do not have to decide. The first day without an arrow is a day for slowness.

You do not need to resolve anything. You have been walking, and that is plenty. If you want a line for the evening, the Sixth Letter has one that Lawrence gives to a friend who had put off starting: "it is better late than never." It is an easy thing to say to yourself at the end of a road.
The questions for tonight:

items.t: What did I notice on this road that I would have walked past on the first morning?
Which of the six days do I most want to read again?
Where, in an ordinary week, could I stop for one breath?

spans.t: A short prayer

Thank you for the road, and for these six days. For the feet that carried me and the mind that kept coming home. Keep what is worth keeping, and let the rest go lightly. Be near on the ordinary days. I will begin again.

Six days is not long, and the book does not ask to be finished. You may have read all of it, stopped at the flat day, or read only the evenings. All of that is fine. This was meant as company on a short road, and a road has no use for a book once it is over, except to be remembered kindly.
So the only question left is what to keep. Not everything. Choose three small things, and keep them light.
What to keep

items.t: A line.
Something Lawrence said, or something said about him, that stayed in your head. It might be the plainest one:
Let us begin, then.

It might be "You tell me nothing new", from the day your mind ran off, or the old man's cheerful admission that he is always saying the same thing. Write it on a card and put it where you will see it.
A turn.

One of the small movements: a breath at a bench, a pause before a chore, a return after you have drifted, a gate closed behind you. Pick the one that cost least and helped most, and do it again tomorrow.
A task.
Choose one thing in your week that you do not like, and decide to do it whole, the way he went over the casks. Not for ever. Once, this week.

spans.t: If one of the three is still with you in a month, the book has done what it was made to do.
Reading Brother Lawrence himself

Go back to him whenever you like. The book we drew on is short, about eleven thousand words, which is an hour or two of reading, and the Letters especially can be taken one at a time, in order, over a few evenings. It is in the public domain, in the same edition we used, at Project Gutenberg as ebook number 13871. Read a letter, and stop when something catches. That is how it was meant to be read.

You will find in it much that is not in these pages: the long self-reproaches, the joys, the letters about sickness. Some of it will not suit you, and some of it may. Read it as you would a letter from a friend of a friend, taking it for what it is, one man's way of living in the company of God, set down in the seventeenth century.

It is fine, too, if little of this fitted. A day may have asked more than you had, or offered less than you hoped. A passage may have seemed strange or beside the point. Leave those, and keep the one that helped.
A last word

Brother Lawrence was a footman who broke things, a soldier, and then a man in a monastery kitchen who was sent to buy the wine. By his own account he found some of that work unwelcome, and at the beginning he spent his hours of prayer in the failing and returning that this book has been about. He did not present himself as a master. As far as the letters show, he thought of himself as someone who had found one small thing that worked and kept repeating it.

That may be the most useful thing to take from him. You do not need to be strong, or certain, or finished. You need a next step, a little patience with yourself, and now and then a remembrance, however brief, that you are not walking alone.
Walk again when you can. And before that, tomorrow, go once round the block at the pace of the road, and see what you pass.
Buen Camino.
